title: Monetary policy statement and Q&A — Christine Lagarde and Boris Vujčić
summary: The ECB kept its three policy rates unchanged on 29 October. A rise was a live option: some members saw a case for acting immediately, before the Council unanimously agreed to wait. Two things had changed since the September projections. Energy prices had exceeded the assumed path, increasing the risk that inflation would stay high long enough to spread. Meanwhile, average ten-year sovereign yields had risen about 35 basis points since the projections’ cut-off, tightening financing conditions before any further Council action. Lagarde indicated that tightening remained the likely direction if the assessment survived the incoming evidence. She gave no commitment on December or on the frequency of future decisions (opening statement and first two monetary-policy exchanges).

The composition of inflation explains why the Council could entertain a hike and still wait. September headline inflation reached 3.8%, up from 3.2% in August, while energy inflation jumped from 14.3% to 18.9%. Elevated refining margins contributed to peaks in petrol and diesel prices. Inflation excluding energy also rose, from 2.1% to 2.3%, and early-stage pricing indicators suggested further pressure. Yet underlying indicators taken together remained broadly stable. The Council could already see energy feeding into other prices. Lagarde saw little evidence that a wage response was adding materially to the second-round effects allowed for in September (‘Inflation’ and opening Q&A).

Compensation per employee had slowed to 3.3% year on year in the second quarter, from 3.6% in the first. Productivity gains cushioned unit labour costs. A separate, forward-looking measure, the ECB wage tracker, pointed to negotiated wage growth of 2.5–2.8% in the remaining months of 2026 and an average of 2.6% in the first three quarters of 2027. Short-horizon inflation expectations had risen, while most longer-horizon measures remained close to 2%. Lagarde expected underlying inflation to become more informative as the shock aged. The December projections, two further inflation readings and third-quarter pay data would therefore help distinguish persistent domestic pressure from energy pass-through (‘Inflation’ and Q&A on the next meeting).

The same energy shock reduced households’ purchasing power and confidence. Incoming data nevertheless suggested that output had expanded in the third quarter. Services had recovered, AI investment was supporting parts of manufacturing and exports, and public infrastructure and defence spending was sustaining demand. The medium-term recovery in private demand depended partly on energy prices easing and real incomes recovering. Further supply disruption, or a cold winter coinciding with low gas storage, could raise inflation while weakening activity. Tighter financial conditions offered a different downside scenario: weaker spending could ultimately reduce inflation (‘Economic activity’ and ‘Risk assessment’).

Transmission was already visible in credit. Banks reported tighter corporate lending standards in the third quarter and declining loan demand despite firms’ greater working-capital needs. In August, firms’ market borrowing cost rose to 4.1% while their bank lending rate remained at 3.8%. Mortgage demand also weakened. Lagarde attributed the global rise in long yields to several possible influences, including inflation expectations, the expected policy path and additional long-dated issuance by large technology firms. She did not quantify their contributions. For portfolios, the distinction matters: a higher sovereign yield can restrain demand even when its rise conveys little about the next policy decision. The reference to a December hike being priced came from a journalist; the transcript supplies no market-implied probability or recommended trade. Separately, Lagarde said she intended to step down after the February 2027 policy meeting and expected continuity in decision-making (‘Financial and monetary conditions’ and Q&A on sovereign yields and succession).

questions.question: What evidence would show energy costs reaching wages strongly enough to change the policy decision?
questions.detail: The ECB identifies upstream price pressure and a moderate wage outlook, but gives no quantitative threshold for a hike. The distinction matters for short-dated euro rates. Compare incoming compensation per employee and negotiated settlements with the October wage tracker, then check productivity and services-price breadth. The ECB wage data and the December staff projections were the most direct next sources available to a researcher at this meeting.

questions.question: How much of the rise in long yields represents an independent tightening of credit?
questions.detail: Lagarde gives the size of the sovereign yield move and several possible explanations. The transcript does not decompose the move or estimate the spending response. If higher term compensation or bond supply drove it, a portfolio positioned for higher policy rates would have a different exposure from one positioned for a steeper curve. Compare dated euro overnight-index swap forwards with sovereign yields, issuance maturities and subsequent bank pricing. Consult the ECB’s market analysis and bank interest-rate statistics.

questions.question: How much tightening was already in the December price before the press conference?
questions.detail: A journalist refers to expectations of a hike, while Lagarde presents a conditional outlook. Neither supplies a probability. This leaves open whether a subsequent confirmation would deliver much additional repricing. Obtain timestamped meeting-dated overnight-index swap quotes immediately before the decision, after the statement and after the Q&A. Check the assumed hike size and contract dates before translating any implied rate change into a probability.
